claims.text: Standard yttrium-free boride components tend to corrode when exposed to molten aluminum.
Adding a small concentration of yttrium to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Yttrium can be incorporated through microalloying or surface modification.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures are approximately 660–750 °C.
Yttrium modification will form a thin, Y-stabilized Al2O3 layer on the boride component surface.
During molten-aluminum exposure, yttrium segregates to the boride surface.
During molten-aluminum exposure, yttrium segregates to grain boundaries in the boride.
Surface and grain-boundary yttrium promotes nucleation of an alumina scale.
Yttrium improves adhesion of the oxide scale.
The Y-enriched oxide barrier is less prone to spallation.
The Y-enriched alumina barrier reduces interdiffusion between the component and molten aluminum.
The Y-enriched alumina barrier slows dissolution of the component in molten aluminum.
Yttrium-modified boride components will exhibit lower weight loss than untreated boride components under molten-aluminum exposure.
Yttrium-modified boride components will exhibit lower corrosion current density than untreated boride components under molten-aluminum exposure.
The beneficial effect should persist over temperatures and exposure durations typical of hot-dip aluminum plating.
Excessive yttrium could compromise mechanical integrity or introduce unwanted phases.
The optimal yttrium concentration is not yet determined.
The long-term stability of the yttrium modification under thermal cycling is uncertain.
A controlled comparison at 700 °C for 100 hours can test the proposed corrosion benefit.

Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement, exemplified by less than a 10% reduction in weight loss or corrosion current density, or failure to form an adherent alumina layer, would falsify the hypothesis.
